a: the LORD
p: 'The LORD' in capitals stands for God's personal name, YHWH, as in most English Bibles.
b: Where the Hebrew has God's name, the four letters YHWH (probably said 'Yahweh'), the Plain English Translation prints "the LORD" in small capitals, following Jewish custom, which reads Adonai, "my Lord," in its place. In the Aramaic chapters (4:8–6:18) the name does not appear; Persian documents and the narrator speak of "the God of the heavens," "the God of Israel" or simply "God" (elaha). The name returns with the Hebrew in 6:21–22.

a: from Jeremiah's mouth
t: The same decree that ends Chronicles
p: 1:1–3 repeats the last verses of 2 Chronicles almost word for word. The few differences are real ones.
b: Ezra opens with the decree that closes 2 Chronicles (2 Chronicles 36:22–23). Where the Hebrew is the same, the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording of Chronicles exactly, so the differences stand out. There are three. Ezra says "from (mippi) Jeremiah's mouth," where Chronicles says "by (befi)," and it spells the prophet's name in its short form, Yirmeyah. In 1:3 Ezra has "May his God be with him" where Chronicles has "the LORD his God" (see the variant there). And Ezra goes on where Chronicles stops: "to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house." Scholars debate which way the copying went; some scholars think the Chronicles ending was added from Ezra to link the books. See the note on 2 Chronicles 36:22.

a: to fulfill the LORD's word
p: Most readers think of Jeremiah's seventy years. Others point to his promise that God would rouse the Medes.
b: The usual answer is Jeremiah's seventy years: "When seventy years are complete for Babylon, I will visit you" (Jeremiah 29:10; compare Jeremiah 25:11–12). 2 Chronicles 36:21 reads it that way. A second answer looks at the verb: Jeremiah also said, "The LORD has roused the spirit of the kings of Media, for his purpose is set against Babylon, to destroy her" (Jeremiah 51:11), using the same phrase "roused the spirit" as this verse. A third adds Jeremiah's promise that the Temple vessels would come back (Jeremiah 27:22), which 1:7–11 tells. The verse may have all three in view. Isaiah's prophecies of Cyrus, which name him (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1), are not mentioned here, though Josephus says Cyrus read them (Antiquities 11.5).
r: Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10; Jeremiah 51:1; Jeremiah 51:11; Jeremiah 27:22; 2 Chronicles 36:21; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1

a: the LORD roused the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia
t: God rouses the king and the people
p: The same verb is used for Cyrus here and for the returning exiles in 1:5. God moves both.
b: The Hebrew verb he'ir means "stir up, wake, rouse." Isaiah uses it of Cyrus: "I myself roused him in righteousness... He will build my city and let my exiles go" (Isaiah 45:13; compare Isaiah 41:2; Isaiah 41:25). Ezra uses it twice in five verses: God rouses the spirit of the king (1:1), and then the spirit of "all those" who go up (1:5). Haggai uses it again when the building starts over: the LORD roused the spirit of Zerubbabel, of Joshua the high priest and of all the people (Haggai 1:14). In Ezra's telling, every new start comes from God moving people's spirits, first a foreign king's and then his own people's.
r: 1:5; Isaiah 41:2; Isaiah 41:25; Isaiah 45:13; Haggai 1:14; 2 Chronicles 36:22; Jeremiah 51:11

a: He sent a proclamation through his whole kingdom, and in writing as well
p: A herald announced the decree aloud, and a written copy was also made. Ezra quotes two versions of it.
b: Literally, "he made a voice pass through all his kingdom." Royal decrees in the ancient Near East were read out by heralds in the local language and also kept in writing. Ezra gives Cyrus's decree twice: here in Hebrew, as a public proclamation addressed to the Jews, and in 6:3–5 in Aramaic, as a dry archive memorandum about the building's size and cost. Elias Bickerman argued in 1946 that these are two genuine forms of one decision, the herald's text and the record kept by the treasury. Others think the Hebrew version was shaped by Jewish writers. See the topic on Cyrus.

a: Cyrus king of Persia says this
p: The decree opens with the formula of Persian royal inscriptions, 'Thus says the king.'
b: "Thus says Darius the king" opens paragraph after paragraph of Darius I's great inscription at Behistun, and Persian royal letters use similar openings. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder found at Babylon in 1879, has Cyrus speak in the first person in the same way: "I am Cyrus, king of the universe, the great king... king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, king of the four quarters." It says Marduk, the god of Babylon, chose him, and that he sent deported peoples back home and restored their gods' shrines. The Cylinder speaks of Mesopotamian cities and never mentions Judah, but it shows the kind of policy and language Ezra describes. The prophets used the same opening, "the LORD says this," for God the great King.

a: the LORD, the God of the heavens
p: Cyrus credits Israel's God with his empire. Was that Persian policy, Jewish shaping, or both?
b: On the Cyrus Cylinder, Cyrus credits Marduk, the god of Babylon, for his victories. Here he credits "the LORD, the God of the heavens." Many historians think both are true to form: a Persian king spoke to each people in terms of its own god, and Jewish officials at court could have drafted a decree for Jews in this way (compare Darius in 6:9–12 and Artaxerxes in 7:12–23). Traditional readers add that Cyrus may have been shown Isaiah's prophecies about him, as Josephus says (Antiquities 11.5–6). Other scholars think the Hebrew wording comes from a Jewish writer retelling the decree. The title "God of the heavens" is typical of the Persian period; the Jews of Elephantine in Egypt used it in their letters to Persian officials about 407 BC.

a: He is the God who is in Jerusalem
t: The God who is in Jerusalem
p: An outsider's way of speaking, perhaps, but it fits the Bible's own idea of the place God chose.
b: The phrase sounds like the language of empire, where each god had a home city: the Cyrus Cylinder speaks of gods returned to "their dwellings." Persian documents in Ezra call him "the God of the heavens" and also place him in Jerusalem (7:19). Jewish readers could hear the same words differently, as an echo of the place the LORD chose "to make his name live there" (Deuteronomy 12:11), the phrase Darius uses in 6:12. The Hebrew can also be read as a confession, "he is the God," with "who is in Jerusalem" naming where his house is. Either way, the decree ties worship of Israel's God to one city.
orig: הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר בִּירוּשָׁלָ‍ִם (hu ha'elohim asher birushalayim)

a: And everyone who is left
p: Either every surviving Jew is to be helped by his neighbors, or the Jews who stay behind are to help those who go.
b: The Hebrew is hard. Kol hannish'ar, "everyone who is left," may be the subject ("every survivor... the people of his place are to help him"), which is how the Plain English Translation reads it. Then the "survivors" are the Jews who outlived the exile, a word the prophets use for the remnant (Nehemiah 1:2–3; Isaiah 10:20–22), and "the people of his place" are their neighbors, Jewish or not. Some read it the other way: "whoever remains behind," that is, Jews who choose to stay in Babylon, are to support those who go. 1:6 says "all the people around them" helped, which fits the first reading and recalls Egypt's gifts in the exodus (see 1:6).

a: the heads of families of Judah and Benjamin
p: The returning community is Judah, Benjamin, the priests and the Levites, yet Ezra calls it Israel.
b: Judah and Benjamin were the tribes of the southern kingdom (1 Kings 12:21), and the Levites served its Temple. Ezra never forgets the twelve tribes: the returnees count "the men of Israel's people" (2:2), call their altar "the altar of Israel's God" (3:2), and offer twelve goats "for all Israel" (6:17; compare 8:35). Ezra–Nehemiah treats this small group as the true heir of all Israel. Some scholars see a claim made against those who stayed in the land; others see a hope that the scattered tribes would rejoin. The phrase "heads of families" (literally "heads of the fathers") names the leaders of the extended family clans.

a: backed them with things made of silver
p: Neighbors load the travelers with silver and gold, as Egypt did when Israel left.
b: The scene recalls the exodus. God had told Moses, "When you go, you will not go empty-handed" (Exodus 3:21), and at the end "They had asked Egypt for silver things and gold things and clothing" (Exodus 12:35). Isaiah had pictured the return from Babylon as a new exodus, led by the LORD and carrying his vessels (Isaiah 52:11–12; compare Isaiah 48:20–21). Ezra does not press the point, but the silver, the gold and the giving neighbors make the echo hard to miss. Literally they "strengthened their hands," a Hebrew idiom for help and encouragement.

a: the vessels belonging to the LORD's house
p: The Temple's gold and silver went to Babylon in stages. Their return links the new Temple to the old one.
b: Nebuchadnezzar carried off the Temple's treasures in 597 and again in 586 BC (2 Kings 24:13; 2 Kings 25:13–17). Chronicles says "He carried everything to Babylon: every article of God's house, big and small" (2 Chronicles 36:18), and Daniel tells of them used at Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5:2–4). Jeremiah had promised: "They will be taken to Babylon, and there they will stay until the day I call for them... Then I will bring them up and return them to this place" (Jeremiah 27:22). The vessels prove that the new house continues the old one, a theme Ezra repeats (5:14–15; 6:5; 7:19; 8:25–34). Persian kings did the same for other peoples: the Cyrus Cylinder says Cyrus returned gods' images to their shrines.
r: 2 Kings 24:13; 2 Kings 25:13–17; 2 Chronicles 36:7; 2 Chronicles 36:10; 2 Chronicles 36:18; Daniel 1:2; Daniel 5:2–4; Jeremiah 27:16–22; 5:14–15; 6:5

a: Mithredath the treasurer
p: Both his name and his title are Persian. The Greek translator did not know the word and simply copied it.
b: Mithredath means "given by Mithra," a Persian god. Gizbar, "treasurer," is a Persian loanword (ganzabara), a title known from documents of the Persian period, including the tablets of the treasury at Persepolis. The Greek translation of Ezra (Rahlfs, checked for this site) did not translate it but wrote gasbarenos, as if it were part of his name. Small details like these, names and titles from the Persian court, are one reason many historians think the author had access to real records.

a: Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah
p: He leads the first return and lays the foundation (5:16), then vanishes. Was he Zerubbabel under another name?
b: Sheshbazzar is a Babylonian name, perhaps Shamash-ab-usur or Sin-ab-usur, "may (the god) protect the father." He is called "leader" (nasi) here and "governor" in 5:14, and 5:16 credits him with laying the foundation, which 3:8–10 credits to Zerubbabel. Some readers, ancient and modern, have taken them as one man with two names, as Daniel had a Babylonian name (Daniel 1:7). Most scholars today think they were two men: Sheshbazzar led the first return under Cyrus, and Zerubbabel came then or later and led the work under Darius. 1 Esdras names both side by side (1 Esdras 6:17). Many identify Sheshbazzar with Shenazzar, a son of King Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:18), which would make him Zerubbabel's uncle, but the names are not the same and the link is uncertain.

a: 29 knives
p: Nobody is sure what this item was. The guesses go back to the ancient translations.
b: The Hebrew machalaphim is found only here. It comes from a root meaning "change, pass through." The Latin Vulgate (cultri) and the KJV took it as "knives" (things that pierce). The Greek of Ezra has parellagmena, "things of a different kind," perhaps "replacements." 1 Esdras 2:12 (KJV) has "censers." The Plain English Translation keeps the traditional "knives" and flags the doubt.

a: The vessels of gold and silver came to 5,400 in all
t: The numbers do not add up
p: The items listed come to 2,499, not 5,400. 1 Esdras has different numbers that do add up.
b: Add the items in 1:9–10 and you get 30 + 1,000 + 29 + 30 + 410 + 1,000 = 2,499. 1 Esdras 2:12–13 gives 1,000 gold cups, 1,000 silver cups, 29 silver censers, 30 gold bowls, 2,410 silver bowls and 1,000 other vessels, which total 5,469, and it gives 5,469 as the sum. Some scholars think 1 Esdras preserves a better list; most think its translator or editor corrected the numbers to make them add up. Others suggest the list names only the main items and the total counts everything. Numbers were easily miscopied in ancient manuscripts, as the differences between Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 also show. See also the variant at 1:10.

a: as the exile was brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem
p: Ezra says nothing of the journey itself, about 900 miles and some four months on foot.
b: Ezra's own journey later took almost four months (7:9). The route ran up the Euphrates and down through Syria, since the desert between Babylon and Judah could not be crossed by a large group. The book skips the journey and the date. Many historians think the first group was small, and that most of the families in chapter 2 came in several waves over the next twenty years. "Went up" ('alah) is the regular Hebrew word for going to Jerusalem, which sits in the hills; the Hebrew Bible's last word in the Jewish order is "let him go up" (2 Chronicles 36:23).

a: the province's people
p: Judah was now a small Persian province, Yehud, inside the huge province Beyond the River.
b: The Hebrew medinah means a district under a governor. Judah had become Yehud, a province of the Persian empire, much smaller than the old kingdom: roughly from Bethel in the north to Beth-zur in the south, about 25 miles across. Jar handles and small silver coins stamped yhd ("Yehud") have been found from the Persian period. The list counts "the province's people," that is, the members of the Jewish community in this Persian district, and shows that Ezra's readers knew themselves as subjects of Persia (compare 5:8; Nehemiah 1:3; Nehemiah 7:6).

a: each to his own town
p: Almost all the towns named lie in Benjamin and northern Judah. The south had been lost to the Edomites.
b: The towns in 2:20–35 (Bethlehem, Anathoth, Ramah, Geba, Michmash, Bethel, Jericho, Lod) are in a small area around Jerusalem, mostly in Benjamin. Hebron and the south are missing. After 586 BC Edomites moved into southern Judah, the region later called Idumea. The list thus fits the real size of Persian Yehud. Families went back to the towns their ancestors had come from, which is why the list mixes family names (2:3–20) with town names (2:21–35).

a: They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua
p: Zerubbabel, of David's royal line, and Jeshua, the high priest's heir, head the list and the story to come.
b: Zerubbabel was a grandson of King Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC (1 Chronicles 3:17–19), so he stood in David's line; his Babylonian name probably means "seed of Babylon." Jeshua (the late form of Joshua) was the son of Jozadak, the priest taken into exile (1 Chronicles 6:15), and the grandson of Seraiah, the chief priest killed by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:18–21). Haggai and Zechariah address them together as governor and high priest (Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 3–4). Ezra does not say when they came. Many scholars think they arrived some years after Sheshbazzar, perhaps early in Darius's reign; see 3:8 and the chapter page.
r: 3:2; 3:8; 4:3; 5:2; 1 Chronicles 3:17–19; 1 Chronicles 6:15; 2 Kings 25:18–21; Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 3:1; Zechariah 4:9

a: Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum and Baanah
p: Nehemiah 7:7 has twelve leaders, one more than Ezra, and several names are spelled differently.
b: The same list in Nehemiah 7:7 adds Nahamani and reads Azariah for Seraiah, Raamiah for Reelaiah, Mispereth for Mispar and Nehum for Rehum. 1 Esdras 5:8 also has twelve names. Many scholars think a name dropped out of Ezra, and that the list once had twelve leaders on purpose, one for each tribe of Israel (compare the twelve goats of 6:17 and 8:35). The Nehemiah and Mordecai named here are almost certainly not the famous ones, who lived about a century later; both names were common.

a: Descendants of Parosh: 2,172.
t: What kind of list is this?
p: A single caravan, several waves of returns, or a census of the whole community? And who copied whom?
b: Read at face value, the list counts those who came back with Zerubbabel and Jeshua under Cyrus, as traditional readers take it. Many scholars think it gathers several returns over the years from 538 to about 520 BC, or later, because it names leaders who came at different times (2:2) and is repeated in Nehemiah's day (Nehemiah 7). Some see it as a register of the whole community of Yehud, compiled for tax or Temple purposes. The same list appears in Nehemiah 7:6–73 and 1 Esdras 5:7–45. Williamson argues that Ezra took it from Nehemiah, since Nehemiah 7:73 and Ezra 3:1 share the same transition; others think Nehemiah took it from Ezra. The chapter page has a table of the differences.

a: Descendants of Adonikam: 666.
p: The number also appears in Solomon's gold and in Revelation. It is a family count here, and Nehemiah has 667.
b: Readers sometimes connect this verse with Solomon's yearly gold, "six hundred and sixty-six talents" (1 Kings 10:14), and with the number of the beast (Revelation 13:18). Nothing in Ezra suggests a symbol: the line simply counts a family, and the parallel list has 667 (Nehemiah 7:18). Adonikam means "my lord has risen." Members of the family came back later with Ezra (8:13).

a: Men of Anathoth: 128.
p: Anathoth was Jeremiah's hometown, where he bought a field as a sign that people would own land there again.
b: Jeremiah was "from among the priests who lived at Anathoth" (Jeremiah 1:1). While Babylon besieged Jerusalem, God told him to buy a family field there and store the deed in a clay jar, because "Houses, fields and vineyards will be bought again in this land" (Jeremiah 32:15). Here 128 men of Anathoth come home. Ezra does not draw the line, but a reader who knows Jeremiah sees the promise kept, as 1:1 invites. Anathoth lay about three miles northeast of Jerusalem, in Benjamin (Joshua 21:18).

a: Descendants of the other Elam: 1,254.
p: Its number is exactly the same as Elam's in 2:7. That may be a copying slip or a real second clan.
b: Nehemiah 7:34 also has "the other Elam" with 1,254, the same figure as Elam in Ezra 2:7 and Nehemiah 7:12. Some scholars think the line is a duplicate that entered the list in copying. Others think there really were two clans with the name, one of them living in a town (the lines around it are town names). The repetition of Harim (2:32; 2:39) and Senaah's huge number, 3,630 (2:35), have also puzzled readers. Senaah may have been a town or a group of people who had no family records.

a: The priests: descendants of Jedaiah
p: The priests number 4,289, about a tenth of the whole community. The Levites number only 74.
b: Four priestly families came back: Jedaiah, Immer, Pashhur and Harim. Jedaiah, Harim and Immer appear among the twenty-four priestly divisions of 1 Chronicles 24:7–14; Pashhur does not. Against these 4,289 priests stand only 74 Levites, plus 128 singers and 139 gatekeepers. Later Ezra could not find a single Levite to join his journey until he sent for them (8:15–20). Levites had lost their place in the Temple's service after Josiah's reform and Ezekiel's rules (Ezekiel 44:10–14), which may explain why few wanted to go. See the topic on the priestly divisions.

a: The singers: descendants of Asaph
p: Chronicles knows three families of singers. This list has only the family of Asaph.
b: In Chronicles, David appoints the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to lead the Temple's music (1 Chronicles 25:1–6). Here only Asaph's descendants appear, and the singers and gatekeepers are listed apart from the Levites, not as Levites. Hartmut Gese (1963) and others have seen in these lists stages in the history of the Temple singers, who were later counted among the Levites, as Chronicles counts them. Others think the list simply reflects who came back. The sons of Asaph lead the singing at the founding of the Temple (3:10).

a: The temple servants
p: The Hebrew calls them netinim, 'the given ones.' Many of their names are foreign.
b: Netinim means "those given," people given to the Temple to do its lowest work. 8:20 says David and his officials gave them to help the Levites. An older tradition traces them to the Gibeonites, whom Joshua made "the ones who cut wood and carried water for the community and for the altar of the LORD" (Joshua 9:27). Several of their names are not Israelite: Meunim (2:50) is the name of an Arab people (2 Chronicles 26:7), Nephusim may be the Ishmaelite Naphish (Genesis 25:15), and Sisera recalls the Canaanite general (Judges 4:2). 1 Chronicles 9:2 calls them "the servants given to the temple." Ezekiel protested against foreigners serving in the sanctuary (Ezekiel 44:7–9).
r: 8:17; 8:20; 7:24; Joshua 9:27; Numbers 31:47; 1 Chronicles 9:2; Nehemiah 10:28; Ezekiel 44:7–9; 2 Chronicles 26:7; Genesis 25:15

a: The descendants of Solomon's servants
p: Perhaps descendants of the foreigners Solomon drafted for forced labor. Some of their names look like job titles.
b: 1 Kings 9:20–21 says Solomon drafted the non-Israelite peoples left in the land as "slave labor," and their descendants may be these "servants of Solomon." They are counted with the temple servants (2:58). Some names look like occupations: Hassophereth means "the scribe" (with the Hebrew article), and Pochereth-hazzebaim (2:57) means "tender of the gazelles." Families that kept a trade over generations could take its name. Nehemiah 11:3 still lists Solomon's servants as a group in Jerusalem.

a: Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan and Immer
p: These are places in Babylonia where exiles lived. Tablets found there show Judeans farming in such villages.
b: Tel means a mound of old ruins: Tel-melah is "mound of salt," and Tel-harsha perhaps "mound of the potsherd" or "of the forest." The exiles were settled in villages on abandoned land, like Tel-abib by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 3:15). About a hundred cuneiform tablets, published in 2014, from a village called Al-Yahudu, "Judah-town," and villages near it, record Judean families from 572 to 477 BC: buying land, paying taxes, and naming children with names that honor the LORD. Later tablets of the Murashu firm at Nippur (about 455–403 BC) also name Jews among its clients.

a: So they were counted unclean and removed from the priesthood
p: Priesthood was inherited. Men who could not prove their descent from Aaron could not serve.
b: Only Aaron's descendants could serve as priests: "If any outsider comes near, he must be put to death" (Numbers 3:10; compare Numbers 16–17). So family records mattered. The Barzillai family had taken the name of David's loyal friend Barzillai the Gileadite (2 Samuel 19:31–39; 1 Kings 2:7) through a marriage, and lost track of their priestly line. The exclusion was not final: they waited for a decision by the Urim and Thummim (2:63). Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, later serves as a priest (8:33; Nehemiah 3:4, 21), which suggests that the Hakkoz family was cleared.
r: Numbers 3:10; Numbers 16:40; 2 Samuel 19:31–39; 1 Kings 2:7; 8:33; Nehemiah 3:4; Nehemiah 3:21; 1 Chronicles 24:10

a: The governor
p: The Hebrew uses a Persian title, Tirshatha. It is later used of Nehemiah.
b: Tirshatha is a Persian word, probably meaning "the one to be respected," something like "His Excellency." It is used of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 8:9; Nehemiah 10:1). Here it probably means Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel, both called governor (5:14; Haggai 1:1). The KJV keeps the word, "the Tirshatha." The Greek of Ezra copies it as Athersatha (checked in Rahlfs), and 1 Esdras 5:40 (KJV) treats it as a person's name, "Nehemias and Atharias."
r: Nehemiah 7:65; Nehemiah 7:70; Nehemiah 8:9; Nehemiah 10:1; 5:14; Haggai 1:1; 1 Esdras 5:40

a: until a priest arose who could use the Urim and the Thummim
p: The sacred lots were no longer in use. The question had to wait, perhaps forever.
b: The Urim and Thummim were objects kept in the high priest's breastpiece for seeking God's decisions: "Put the Urim and the Thummim into the breastpiece for decisions" (Exodus 28:30). They are not mentioned in use after David's time. The governor's ruling assumes they were not available, and Jewish tradition says they never returned: the Mishnah says they ceased when "the former prophets" died (Mishnah Sotah 9:12), and the Talmud lists them among five things the second Temple lacked (Bavli Yoma 21b). The Greek translators guessed at their meaning: "for those who give light and the perfect ones" (Rahlfs, checked).

a: Taken together, the whole assembly was 42,360,
t: A total that is too big
p: The family numbers add up to 29,818 here and 31,089 in Nehemiah. Both books give the same total, 42,360.
b: Add every number in 2:3–60 and you get 29,818. The same list in Nehemiah 7 adds up to 31,089. Yet both books give the same total, 42,360, and so does the Greek of 1 Esdras 5:41 (the KJV of that verse splits it into "forty thousand, beside menservants and womenservants two thousand three hundred and sixty"). Many explanations have been offered. The total may include groups the list does not itemize, such as women, or Israelites of the northern tribes, or families who had lost their records. It may come from a separate census. Or the family numbers may have suffered in copying while the total, easy to remember, did not. The two lists differ in about twenty of their numbers (see the table on the chapter page), so copying errors are certain in some places. 1 Esdras 5:41–42 also has its own figures for what follows: 7,347 slaves, 245 singers, 7,036 horses and 5,525 beasts of burden.

a: male and female slaves
p: The Hebrew eved can mean a servant or a slave. Here they are household slaves, about one for every six free people.
b: Eved covers a wide range, from a royal minister ("the king's servant") to a slave who could be bought. These 7,337 men and women owned by the returning families are slaves; the word is the same as "Solomon's servants" in 2:55, where the Plain English Translation uses "servants." Slavery was common across the Persian empire, and Babylonian contracts of the time record the sale of household slaves. Nehemiah later protested when poor Jews were forced to sell their own children (Nehemiah 5:1–8). The 200 singers here are probably entertainers for feasts, distinct from the Temple singers of 2:41.

a: 61,000 drachmas of gold
p: The coin named is either the Greek drachma or the Persian daric. Nehemiah's version of the gifts is quite different.
b: The Hebrew darkemonim is usually taken as the Greek silver drachma, though here it is gold; others take it as the Persian gold daric, first minted by Darius I about 515 BC, which would be a later writer's way of stating the value. A mina was about 1.25 pounds of silver. Nehemiah 7:70–72 divides the gifts among the governor, the family heads and the people, and its totals differ: 41,000 drachmas of gold, 4,200 minas of silver and 597 priests' robes, plus 50 bowls. 1 Esdras 5:44 (KJV) has 1,000 pounds of gold, 5,000 of silver and 100 vestments. The gifts echo the freewill offerings of the tabernacle (Exodus 35:20–29).

a: All Israel lived in their towns.
p: Nehemiah 7:73 ends the same list with the same words, then goes on, 'and the seventh month came,' just like Ezra 3:1.
b: The parallel list in Nehemiah closes: "The priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, some of the people, the temple servants and all Israel made their homes in their towns. The seventh month arrived. The Israelites were in their towns" (Nehemiah 7:73). Ezra 3:1 continues with the same words. In Nehemiah the seventh month leads to Ezra's reading of the law (Nehemiah 8); in Ezra it leads to the altar. Many scholars take this shared seam as proof that one book borrowed the list from the other along with its ending, though they disagree on which way the borrowing went.

a: The seventh month arrived.
p: The seventh month, Tishri (September to October), held the Day of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Booths.
b: Ezra does not say which year; the story implies the first autumn after the return, perhaps 538 or 537 BC. The seventh month was the busiest month of Israel's calendar: a day of trumpet blasts on the first, the Day of Atonement on the tenth, and the Feast of Booths from the fifteenth (Leviticus 23:23–43). Solomon had dedicated the first Temple in this month (1 Kings 8:2). "As one" (literally "as one man") describes a people united in purpose, as in Judges 20:1 and Nehemiah 8:1. On the shared wording with Nehemiah 7:73, see 2:70.
r: Leviticus 23:23–43; Numbers 29:1–38; 1 Kings 8:2; Nehemiah 7:73; Nehemiah 8:1; Judges 20:1

a: Jeshua son of Jozadak
p: Jeshua is the Joshua of Haggai and Zechariah. In Greek his name is Iesous, the same name as Jesus.
b: Jeshua is the late Hebrew form of Joshua. Haggai and Zechariah call him "Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest" (Haggai 1:1). In Zechariah's visions he stands before the angel of the LORD in filthy clothes and is clothed in clean ones (Zechariah 3:1–5), and a crown is made for him (Zechariah 6:11). His family led the priesthood until the second century BC (Nehemiah 12:10–11). The Greek writes his name Iesous, as it does for Joshua son of Nun and for Jesus, and early Christians such as Justin Martyr read Zechariah's Joshua as a figure of Christ (Dialogue with Trypho 115–116). His sons later married foreign wives (10:18).
r: Haggai 1:1; Haggai 2:2; Zechariah 3:1–10; Zechariah 6:11–13; Nehemiah 12:10–11; 1 Chronicles 6:15; 10:18

a: Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel
t: Son of Shealtiel or of Pedaiah?
p: Ezra, Haggai and Matthew call Zerubbabel Shealtiel's son. The Hebrew of 1 Chronicles 3:19 makes him the son of Pedaiah.
b: 1 Chronicles 3:17–19 lists Jehoiachin's sons, Shealtiel and Pedaiah among them, and then says "Pedaiah's sons: Zerubbabel and Shimei" (1 Chronicles 3:19). Everywhere else Zerubbabel is "son of Shealtiel" (Haggai 1:1; Nehemiah 12:1; Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27). Three explanations are common. Shealtiel may have died childless, and his brother Pedaiah fathered a son in his name, by the law of the brother-in-law (Deuteronomy 25:5–6). Zerubbabel may have been adopted or reckoned as Shealtiel's heir. Or the Chronicles text may have suffered in copying; the Greek of 1 Chronicles 3:19 reads "Salathiel," that is, Shealtiel. All agree he was Jehoiachin's grandson.
r: 1 Chronicles 3:17–19; Haggai 1:1; Haggai 2:23; Nehemiah 12:1; Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27; Deuteronomy 25:5–6

a: They built the altar of Israel's God
p: Sacrifice came before the building. Some worship may have gone on at the ruined site all through the exile.
b: The returnees rebuild the altar before they lay the Temple's foundation, as Abraham built altars in the land before any house existed, and as David built one on Araunah's threshing floor before the Temple was planned (2 Samuel 24:25). The burnt offerings start at once (3:6). Some offering may never have stopped: soon after 586 BC, eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria; the text says "They had grain offerings and frankincense in their hands to bring to the house of the LORD" (Jeremiah 41:5, translated fresh), which suggests the ruined site was still a place of worship. The Talmud says three prophets came back with the exiles, one of whom testified where the altar had stood (Bavli Zevachim 62a).

a: the law of Moses the man of God
p: The return is shaped from the start by the written law. 'The man of God' is Moses' title in Deuteronomy 33:1.
b: The Hebrew torah, "law," means "instruction, teaching" as well as a code of rules. Ezra–Nehemiah stresses doing things "as it is written" (3:4; 6:18; Nehemiah 8:14–15; Nehemiah 10:34–36). Here the law's rules for burnt offerings are in view: "two yearling lambs, every day, without fail" (Exodus 29:38; compare Numbers 28:3–8). Moses is called "the man of God" in the blessing of Deuteronomy: "Before his death, Moses the man of God blessed the Israelites" (Deuteronomy 33:1), and in the title of Psalm 90. The book takes for granted a written Torah of Moses that everyone accepts, long before Ezra the scribe arrives with it (7:6, 10). Critical scholars debate how much of the five books had reached their final form by 538 BC.

a: because dread of the peoples of the lands was on them
p: The Hebrew 'for' can give the reason for building the altar, or the danger they faced as they built.
b: The Hebrew says simply "for (ki) dread was on them." Read as a reason, the people set up the altar quickly because they were afraid, seeking God's protection through regular sacrifice. Read as a concession, as many translations do, they built it in spite of their fear. 1 Esdras 5:49 tells it more fully: some from the other nations of the land gathered to them, and they set up the altar because all the nations of the land were hostile to them. "The peoples of the lands," in the plural, is Ezra–Nehemiah's name for the populations around the returnees, a group that grows sharper in 4:4 and 9:1–2. "On its old base" (literally "on its stands") means the altar went back on its original site.

a: They held the Feast of Booths just as it is written.
p: The law set a falling number of bulls for each day of the feast, from thirteen down to seven.
b: Booths (Sukkot) was the autumn harvest feast, when Israel lived in shelters to remember the wilderness (Leviticus 23:42–43). Numbers 29:12–38 sets out its sacrifices "the number set by the rule for each day": thirteen bulls on the first day, twelve on the second, down to seven on the seventh, with rams and lambs, then a closing day. Solomon dedicated his Temple at this feast (1 Kings 8:2, 65), and Nehemiah 8:14–18 tells of a later celebration, when the people lived in booths as they had not since Joshua's days. See the topic on the Feast of Booths.
r: Leviticus 23:33–43; Numbers 29:12–38; Deuteronomy 16:13–15; 1 Kings 8:2; Nehemiah 8:14–18; Zechariah 14:16

a: the regular burnt offering
p: The tamid was the lamb offered every morning and every evening, the heartbeat of Temple worship.
b: Olat tamid means "the continual burnt offering," a lamb each morning and evening with flour, oil and wine (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–8). The Mishnah devotes a whole tractate, Tamid, to how it was offered. In Daniel the stopping of "the regular offering" marks the worst disaster (Daniel 8:11; Daniel 11:31). Here its restoration marks a new beginning, even before the Temple has walls. The verse moves from the daily offering to the monthly and yearly ones, and then to gifts that individuals chose to give.

a: to bring cedar wood from Lebanon to the sea at Joppa
p: The second Temple is supplied the way the first one was, with Lebanese cedar floated down the coast to Joppa.
b: Solomon paid Hiram of Tyre in food and oil for cedar from Lebanon (1 Kings 5:9–11). Chronicles has Hiram promise, "We will bring it to you on the sea, tied in rafts, to Joppa, and you can carry it up to Jerusalem" (2 Chronicles 2:16). Ezra echoes those details on purpose: the new house is built like the old. In the Persian period the coast was in the hands of Sidon and Tyre. The inscription on the coffin of Eshmunazar, king of Sidon in the fifth century BC, says the "lord of kings," the Persian king, gave him Dor and Joppa. Joppa is modern Jaffa, beside Tel Aviv.

a: In the second year after they came to God's house in Jerusalem
p: Ezra puts the foundation under Cyrus. Haggai and Zechariah seem to put it in 520 BC, under Darius.
b: This verse puts the start of the work in the spring of the second year after the return, about 536 BC. 5:16 says Sheshbazzar laid the foundations under Cyrus. But Haggai dates the day "the LORD's temple was founded" to the twenty-fourth of the ninth month of Darius's second year, December 520 BC (Haggai 2:18), and Zechariah says "Zerubbabel's own hands founded this house" (Zechariah 4:9). Many traditional readers see two stages: a start under Cyrus, then a stop (4:24), then a fresh founding in 520. Many critical scholars think the writer of Ezra 3 has placed the work of 520 in Cyrus's time, joining Zerubbabel and Sheshbazzar into one story. Others note that "found" (yasad) can mean "restore, repair," so both texts could describe stages of one project.

a: twenty years old and up
p: The law set the Levites' age of service at thirty or twenty-five. After the exile it was twenty.
b: Numbers counts Levites for service "from thirty years old and up" (Numbers 4:3) and also says "from twenty-five years old and up, a man will come to join the work force" (Numbers 8:24). Chronicles has David lower the age to twenty (1 Chronicles 23:24, 27; compare 2 Chronicles 31:17). Ezra's community follows the latest rule, perhaps because there were so few Levites (2:40). Commentators see in the different ages a practice that changed over time as the need for workers changed.

a: as David king of Israel had arranged
p: Trumpets for priests, cymbals for Levites: the music follows the pattern Chronicles credits to David.
b: Literally, "by the hands of David." In Chronicles David appoints Levite singers with cymbals, harps and lyres, and priests with trumpets, when the ark comes to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:16–24; 1 Chronicles 16:4–6), and he organizes the singers for the future Temple (1 Chronicles 25). The same pattern appears at Solomon's dedication (2 Chronicles 5:12–13) and Hezekiah's rededication (2 Chronicles 29:25–28). By using it here, Ezra presents the new Temple's worship as continuous with David's. The founding is celebrated like a completion, perhaps because the people believed the house was as good as built.
r: 1 Chronicles 15:16–24; 1 Chronicles 16:4–6; 1 Chronicles 25:1–8; 2 Chronicles 5:12–13; 2 Chronicles 29:25–28; Nehemiah 12:24; Nehemiah 12:36

a: For he is good, for his loyal love over Israel is forever.
p: The refrain of Solomon's dedication, with 'over Israel' added. Jeremiah had said it would be heard again.
b: The words repeat the refrain sung when the ark entered Solomon's Temple: "For he is good, for his loyal love is forever" (2 Chronicles 5:13; compare 1 Chronicles 16:34; Psalm 136:1). Only Ezra adds "over Israel." The scene also answers a prophecy. In ruined Jerusalem Jeremiah promised that there would again be heard "the sound of those who say, 'Give thanks to the LORD of Armies, for the LORD is good, for his loyal love is forever,' and of those who bring a thank offering to the LORD's house" (Jeremiah 33:11, translated fresh). Hesed, "loyal love," is God's faithfulness to his covenant; see the topic.
r: 2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3; 1 Chronicles 16:34; Psalm 136:1; Psalm 106:1; Jeremiah 33:10–11

a: old enough to have seen the first house
p: The Temple had been burned about fifty years before. The old men remembered it, and Haggai asks them to compare.
b: Solomon's Temple was burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9), about fifty years before this scene, so these men were at least in their sixties. Haggai addresses the same people some years later: "Who is left among you who saw this house in its first glory? How do you see it now? Is it not like nothing in your eyes?" (Haggai 2:3). Josephus says the old men wept because the new building was so much poorer than the old (Antiquities 11.80–83). Some readers think the tears were of joy as well as grief. Either way the book does not take sides: weeping and shouting rise together (3:13).

a: No one could tell the glad shouting apart from the weeping of the people
p: The chapter ends with a sound that is both. Readers have heard in it the whole mood of the return.
b: The Hebrew keeps hammering the same words: sound, shout, joy, weeping, people, heard. Tamara Eskenazi and other literary readers see the verse as a picture of the whole community, joined in one sound though its feelings differ. Jewish readers have linked it with the mixed joy of later restorations, and with the custom of remembering Jerusalem's ruin even at weddings (compare Psalm 137:5–6). Christian readers have often read it as an image of hope that is real but not yet complete, a theme Haggai develops: "The last glory of this house will be greater than the first" (Haggai 2:9).

a: Judah and Benjamin's enemies
p: The narrator calls them enemies before they speak. They describe themselves as worshipers of Israel's God.
b: The label comes first: tsare, "adversaries." Then the people speak for themselves: they seek the same God and have sacrificed to him for generations (4:2). They were descendants of peoples the Assyrians had settled in the former northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:24), and probably Israelites who had stayed in the land as well. Josephus calls them Cuthaeans, his name for the Samaritans (Antiquities 11.19–20, 84–88), and many later readers have done the same. Many scholars today caution that a separate Samaritan community, with its own temple on Mount Gerizim, took shape later, in the fifth century BC at the earliest. Ezra–Nehemiah tells the story from the returnees' side only. See the topic on the Samaritans.

a: Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who brought us up here
p: Kings tells of settlers brought in after 722 BC. These people trace their arrival to Esarhaddon, a generation later.
b: After Samaria fell in 722 BC, "the king of Assyria brought in people from Babylon, from Cuthah, from Avva, from Hamath and Sepharvaim. He settled them in Samaria's towns" (2 Kings 17:24). That was Sargon II. Esarhaddon reigned from 681 to 669 BC, and his own inscriptions tell of deporting peoples from one end of his empire to the other, so a further settlement in his time is likely, though no text outside Ezra records it here. 4:10 names yet another settlement by Osnappar. Isaiah 7:8 has been linked to such a later deportation. Kings says these settlers "feared the LORD" but also served their own gods (2 Kings 17:33), which is how the returnees saw them.

a: It is not for you and us to build a house for our God.
p: Zerubbabel says no. Readers have judged the refusal as faithfulness, as legal caution, or as exclusion.
b: A religious reading, traditional in both Judaism and Christianity: the offer came from people whose worship was mixed (2 Kings 17:33), and sharing the building would have meant sharing the Temple. A legal reading: Cyrus's permission was given to the exiles (1:3), and Zerubbabel's words "as King Cyrus... commanded us" point to the decree, so outsiders had no standing. A critical reading, held by Blenkinsopp, Grabbe and others: the returnees claimed to be the only true Israel and shut out Judeans and northerners who had never left, and the story is told to justify that claim. The book itself later welcomes anyone who separates from the uncleanness of the nations to seek the LORD (6:21), which complicates every reading.

a: the people of the land
p: In Kings the phrase means Judah's own citizens. In Ezra it means the population the returnees found when they came.
b: Am ha'arets in 2 Kings means the landholding people of Judah, who crown kings in a crisis (2 Kings 11:14; 2 Kings 21:24; 2 Kings 23:30). In Ezra–Nehemiah the phrase and its plural, "the peoples of the land(s)," name the mixed population outside the returnee community (3:3; 9:1–2; 10:2; Nehemiah 10:30–31). That probably included Judeans whose families were never deported, as well as northerners and foreigners. Later, in the rabbis' usage, am ha'arets came to mean someone careless about the law's details (Mishnah Avot 2:5). Readers should not assume the phrase means foreigners only; that is one of the book's open questions.

a: worked to break the courage of the people of Judah
p: Literally 'weakening the hands,' an idiom for destroying morale. The same phrase turns up in a letter from Lachish.
b: The Hebrew says they were "making the hands of the people of Judah slack." The idiom means to sap someone's will to work or fight. Jeremiah's enemies used it against him: the officials said he was "weakening the hands of the fighting men" (Jeremiah 38:4). A letter written on a potsherd at Lachish just before 586 BC (Lachish Letter 6) uses the same phrase of the officials in Jerusalem, whose words "weaken the hands." The opposite idiom, "strengthen the hands," is used for the help in 1:6 and 6:22.

a: In the reign of Ahasuerus
p: 4:6–23 leaps ahead to Xerxes and Artaxerxes, decades after Zerubbabel, then 4:24 returns to Darius.
b: Ahasuerus is Xerxes I (486–465 BC), the king of Esther, and Artaxerxes is Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC). Their letters concern the city and its walls (4:12), not the Temple, and they come after the events of chapters 5–6. Most commentators, traditional and critical alike (Kidner, Williamson, Fensham, Blenkinsopp), think the writer gathered all the opposition into one place by theme, to show that resistance lasted from Cyrus to Artaxerxes, and then went back to the story in 4:24. An older harmonizing view took Ahasuerus as Cambyses and Artaxerxes as the usurper Bardiya (Smerdis), so that the letters fall before Darius. Josephus already set the letter under Cambyses (Antiquities 11.21–30). 1 Esdras puts it between Cyrus's decree and Darius (1 Esdras 2:15–25).

a: Bishlam
p: Bishlam may be a name, a word meaning 'with the approval of,' or a scribal slip for 'against Jerusalem.'
b: The KJV, ESV and most translations take Bishlam as a man's name, and 1 Esdras 2:15 (KJV) has "Belemus." But bishlam can be read as "in peace" or "with the agreement of": the Greek of Ezra translates "he wrote in peace" (en eirene, checked in Rahlfs). Some scholars read "with the approval of Mithredath," making Mithredath the senior official. Others think the word is a copying slip for al-Yerushalem, "against Jerusalem," as in 4:8. The verb "wrote" is singular, which suggests one main writer.

a: translated into Aramaic
p: The Hebrew ends with the word 'Aramaic' a second time. Many take it as a note: 'What follows is in Aramaic.'
b: Word for word the verse ends: "and the writing of the letter was written in Aramaic and translated: Aramaic." The first "Aramaic" probably refers to the script, and "translated" to the language. The final aramit may belong with that, "translated into Aramaic," as the Plain English Translation takes it, or it may be a heading telling the reader that the text now changes language, as the same word does in Daniel 2:4. Either way, from 4:8 to 6:18 the book is written in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire, and returns to Hebrew at 6:19.
orig: כָּתוּב אֲרָמִית וּמְתֻרְגָּם אֲרָמִית (katuv aramit umetugam aramit)

a: wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes against Jerusalem
p: 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26 are in Aramaic, the language Persian officials used across their empire.
b: Aramaic, a sister language of Hebrew, was spoken in Syria and became the shared written language of the Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian empires. Judah's officials already knew it in 701 BC: "Please, talk to us, your servants, in Aramaic. We can understand it" (2 Kings 18:26). Persian scribes wrote letters in it from Egypt to Afghanistan, and the papyri of the Jewish garrison at Elephantine in Egypt are in the same kind of Aramaic as these chapters. Ezra keeps the language of the documents and even continues in Aramaic for the story between them (4:23–24; 5:1–5; 6:13–18). The other Aramaic passages in the Bible are Daniel 2:4–7:28, Jeremiah 10:11 and two words in Genesis 31:47. On the chapter page, see the box on the letters.

a: Rehum the chief official and Shimshai the scribe
p: Rehum's title, 'master of decree,' is a known Persian-era office, the official in charge of reports.
b: Be'el te'em, literally "master of the decree" or "of the report," comes from an Akkadian title, bel temi. It names a senior official who issued orders and sent reports; the KJV has "chancellor." A similar title appears in the Aramaic letters of Arshama, the Persian governor of Egypt, in the late fifth century BC. Shimshai's title, safra, is "scribe" or "secretary," the man who wrote the letter. Their base was Samaria (4:17). The pair writes on behalf of a long list of officials and settled peoples (4:9–10), as letters to the king often named everyone who joined in.

a: the judges, envoys and officials, the Persians
p: Older translations read these words as names of peoples. Most now read several of them as Persian titles.
b: The KJV, following the Greek and the Masoretic vowels, lists peoples: "the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites." The Greek of Ezra (Rahlfs, checked) also has a row of peoples. Most scholars now think the first words are Persian and Akkadian titles: dinaya, "judges"; afarsatkaya, perhaps "envoys" or "inspectors"; tarpelaya, "officials" (or possibly people from Tripolis); and afarsaya, "Persians" or another title. The rest are clearly places: Erech (Uruk), Babylon, and Susa in Elam. Every proposal is uncertain, and the Plain English Translation's choices are only the most common ones.

a: Osnappar, the great and honored
p: The last great king of Assyria, who crushed Babylon and Elam and deported their people.
b: No Assyrian king is called Osnappar, but most scholars identify him with Ashurbanipal (669–about 631 BC). He put down his brother's revolt in Babylon in 648 BC and sacked Susa, the Elamite capital, about 646 BC, which fits the Babylonians, Susians and Elamites of 4:9. The name may have been worn down in copying: the Greek of Ezra has Asennaphar (Rahlfs, checked), and 1 Esdras does not mention him. The NIV prints "Ashurbanipal"; the Plain English Translation keeps the Aramaic name and explains it here. Calling an Assyrian king "great and honored" is the polite style of the letter's writers, whose ancestors he had moved.

a: Beyond the River
p: The Persian province west of the Euphrates, from Syria to the border of Egypt.
b: Abar-nahara, "beyond the river," looks west across the Euphrates from Mesopotamia, where the empire was run. It was the name of a great province covering Syria, Phoenicia, Samaria, Judah and the coast. In Akkadian it is Ebir-nari. From Cyrus on it was joined to Babylon under one satrap; it became a separate satrapy under Xerxes. The same phrase is used for the lands Solomon ruled in 1 Kings 4:24 (5:4 in Hebrew) and in Nehemiah 2:7. Judah was a small district inside it, and Samaria another.

a: And now:
p: Aramaic letters open with an address and then 'and now' before the business. Ezra keeps the formula.
b: The Aramaic uke'enet (4:10, 4:11) and ukhe'en (4:17) mean "and now." In Aramaic letters of the Persian period, such as those from Elephantine, this word divides the opening, who writes to whom with a greeting, from the body of the letter. Older translations sometimes took it as "and so on" ("at such a time," KJV), as if an editor had cut a list short. The Plain English Translation keeps "And now:" so the reader can see the shape of a real letter: address (4:11), body (4:12–16); address and greeting, "Peace" (4:17), body (4:18–22).

a: They are building the rebellious and evil city.
p: This complaint is about the city and its walls, under Artaxerxes I, long after the Temple was finished.
b: The Temple was finished in 515 BC (6:15). This letter, under Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC), accuses the Jews of rebuilding Jerusalem's walls. It is probably the same campaign of wall-building that was stopped "with force and might" (4:23), and it may explain the news that broke Nehemiah's heart in 445 BC: "Jerusalem's wall is breached, and fire has burned its gates" (Nehemiah 1:3). The date may fit a time of unrest in the west, when Egypt revolted (about 460–454 BC) and the governor Megabyzus rebelled, making the king nervous about fortified towns. Some link the wall work to Ezra's own arrival in 458 BC (7:1–9).

a: in the end it will do harm to the kings
p: The word behind 'in the end' is Persian and uncertain. It may mean 'revenue' instead.
b: Appetom appears only here. It is a Persian loanword, and scholars disagree on its sense. Some take it as "in the end, surely": "in the end it will harm the kings," as the Plain English Translation has it. Others take it as "revenue, treasury": "the royal revenue will suffer." The threat is the same either way: an independent Jerusalem would stop paying the king. The three taxes are named with Akkadian words: mindah, tribute; belo, a tax on produce or a poll tax; and halakh, a land tax or service duty. Artaxerxes later exempts Temple staff from all three (7:24).

a: we eat the palace's salt
p: An idiom for loyalty: those who live on the king's provisions owe him faithful service.
b: To eat someone's salt meant to share his table and so to owe him loyalty; Persian and Arabic still use the idiom. Salt also sealed agreements in the Bible: Chronicles speaks of the kingship given to David "by a covenant of salt" (2 Chronicles 13:5), and Numbers of the priests' share as "a covenant of salt for all time" (Numbers 18:19). The officials present their complaint as an act of duty, not of spite. A popular claim that the English word "salary" comes from soldiers paid in salt is doubtful and has nothing to do with this verse.

a: your fathers' record book
p: Persian kings saw themselves as heirs of Babylon's kings, whose records described Jerusalem's revolts.
b: The "fathers" are the king's predecessors, including the Babylonian kings before Cyrus. Jerusalem had rebelled against Assyria under Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:7) and against Babylon twice, under Jehoiakim and Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:1; 2 Kings 24:20). The Babylonian Chronicle, a set of cuneiform tablets, records Nebuchadnezzar's capture of "the city of Judah" in 597 BC. The search ordered in 4:19 would have found such records, just as Darius's search found Cyrus's memorandum (6:1–2). The accusers' history is accurate; their prediction about tribute was the exaggeration.

a: read out in my presence and explained
p: The word may mean 'clearly,' 'section by section,' or 'translated.' The rabbis read its Hebrew twin as translation.
b: Meparash comes from a root meaning "separate, make distinct." It may mean the letter was read "clearly" or "paragraph by paragraph," or that it was translated from Aramaic into Persian for the king. Persian court practice favored the last: documents were drafted in Aramaic and read aloud in the king's language. The same word in Hebrew describes Ezra's public reading of the law, "explaining it as they went. They set out its meaning" (Nehemiah 8:8). The Talmud took that verse to mean translation into Aramaic, the origin of the Targum (Bavli Megillah 3a).

a: until I give the order
p: The king stops the building for now, but leaves room for a later decree. Nehemiah would get it.
b: Artaxerxes does not forbid the city forever. He says it is not to be built "until I give the order." The same king later sends Nehemiah with letters to rebuild the walls (Nehemiah 2:1–8). Daniel and Esther speak of "the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot pass away" (Daniel 6:8, translated fresh; compare Esther 1:19; Esther 8:8), but this decree is careful to leave the king free to change his mind. Many readers see the hand of God in the wording, as Ezra does when "the good hand of his God" is on Ezra (7:9) and Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:8).

a: until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia
t: Darius I and the year 520 BC
p: The story returns from the walls to the Temple. Darius's second year was 520 BC.
b: After the parenthesis of 4:6–23, the narrative picks up from 4:5. Darius I took the throne in 522 BC after the death of Cambyses and the brief reign of a man who claimed to be Cyrus's son Bardiya; Darius spent his first year putting down revolts, as his inscription at Behistun boasts. His second year, 520 BC, is when Haggai and Zechariah begin to prophesy (Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 1:1). The opening word "Then" links this verse to 4:23 in a loose way. A few older readers took this Darius as Darius II (423–404 BC), so that the order would be strictly chronological, but Haggai's dates rule that out.

a: Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo
p: Their own books date their words to 520–518 BC and show what they told the builders.
b: Haggai's four short messages are dated between August and December 520 BC. He blamed the people's poor harvests on the neglected house: "Is this a time for you, yes you, to live in houses covered with wood, while this house is desolate?" (Haggai 1:4). Zechariah, whose first message came that autumn and whose night visions followed in February 519 BC, promised: "Zerubbabel's own hands founded this house, and his hands will bring it to completion" (Zechariah 4:9). Zechariah 1:1 calls him "son of Berechiah, son of Iddo"; Ezra names the better-known grandfather, the head of a priestly family that came back with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 12:4; Nehemiah 12:16). Their books are in the Book of the Twelve, the last part of the Prophets.
r: 6:14; Haggai 1:1–15; Haggai 2:1–23; Zechariah 1:1; Zechariah 4:6–10; Zechariah 8:9; Nehemiah 12:4; Nehemiah 12:16

a: who was over them
t: The God who was over them
p: The phrase may mean God was their ruler and protector, or that his name had been called over them.
b: The Aramaic says they prophesied "in the name of the God of Israel, upon them." It may mean the God who watched over them, or it may echo a Hebrew phrase about a people who belong to God: "Every people on earth will see that the LORD's name has been called over you" (Deuteronomy 28:10; compare Jeremiah 14:9). A third reading takes "upon them" with "prophesied," that is, "prophesied to them." The Plain English Translation gives the most common reading.
orig: בְּשֻׁם אֱלָהּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עֲלֵיהוֹן (beshum elah Yisra'el 'alehon)

a: began to build God's house in Jerusalem
p: Haggai dates the restart to the twenty-fourth of the sixth month, September 520 BC.
b: Haggai's first message came on the first day of the sixth month (Haggai 1:1), and the people began work on the twenty-fourth of the same month (Haggai 1:14–15), about three weeks later. Ezra gives no dates here but keeps the same pair of leaders and credits the prophets with "helping" (literally "supporting") the builders. Only later does Persian permission catch up (5:3–6:12). The book's pattern is that God's word through the prophets moves first, and the king's word confirms it (6:14).

a: Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River
p: A cuneiform tablet of 502 BC names Tattenai as governor of Beyond the River, a real official.
b: A Babylonian business document dated in Darius's twentieth year (502 BC) mentions "Tattannu, governor of Beyond the River" (published by Ungnad, Vorderasiatische Schriftdenkmäler 4, no. 152, and discussed by Olmstead). In those years Babylon and Beyond the River formed one great satrapy, so Tattenai was a governor serving under the satrap, in charge of the western lands. His visit to Jerusalem is what a careful official would do when a large building went up without papers on file. Shethar-bozenai has a Persian name and may have been a secretary or inspector. The tablet is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that Ezra's account of the Persian officials rests on real knowledge.

a: complete these fittings
p: The Aramaic word is rare. It may mean the fittings and materials, the woodwork, or the whole structure.
b: Ushsharna is not found elsewhere in the Bible. In Aramaic papyri from Egypt a similar word is used for materials and equipment, such as the wood and fittings for repairing a boat. So the officials may be asking about the timber work and furnishings (compare 5:8, where they note the beams in the walls) rather than the whole structure, which is why the Plain English Translation says "fittings." Others take it as "this structure," "this wall" or "this sanctuary." The Greek of Ezra has choregia, "provision, supply" (Rahlfs, checked), which fits the "materials" reading.

a: But their God kept his eye on the elders of the Jews.
p: God's watchful care protected the builders while the slow Persian paperwork went to the king and back.
b: The eye of God is a picture of attention and protection: the land of promise is "a land the LORD your God looks after. The eyes of the LORD your God are always on it" (Deuteronomy 11:12; compare Psalm 33:18). Ezra later speaks of God's "hand" in the same way (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31). The officials do not stop the work while they wait for an answer, which may simply be good administration. The book sees God behind it. Note that the leaders are now "the elders of the Jews," a council of family heads. In the Elephantine papyri, too, the leaders of a Jewish community write as a group to Persian officials.

a: Here is a copy of the letter
p: Many historians accept the Aramaic letters as real Persian documents, perhaps lightly edited. Others doubt them.
b: For genuineness: Eduard Meyer (1896) argued that the letters fit what was known of Persian rule, and finds since then have supported many details: the officials' titles, the Aramaic of the period, the "and now" form of letters (4:10), the memorandum format (6:2), and the real governor Tattenai (5:3). Williamson, Fensham and Blenkinsopp accept the documents in substance. Against: C. C. Torrey (1910) called them Jewish inventions; more recently Lester Grabbe and Dirk Schwiderski have argued that their greeting formulas and spelling belong to a later, Hellenistic stage of Aramaic, and that they flatter the Jews in ways real officials would not. Middle positions are common: genuine originals, updated in spelling and shaped as they were copied into the story. The word for "copy," parshegen, is itself a Persian loanword.

a: To Darius the king: all peace.
p: A short greeting, as in Persian-period letters. The body begins in the next verse with 'Let it be known.'
b: Aramaic letters of the period open with the addressee and a greeting of shelam, "peace, well-being." Letters to a superior at Elephantine wish "the welfare of our lord" at length; a letter to the king uses a short formula, as here. Tattenai's letter then follows the standard pattern: report of what was seen (5:8), questions asked and answers given (5:9–16), and a request for a decision (5:17). Compare the shorter "Peace" of 4:17. The KJV, keeping the Aramaic word order, has "Unto Darius the king, all peace."
orig: לְדָרְיָוֶשׁ מַלְכָּא שְׁלָמָא כֹלָּא (ledaryavesh malka shelama kholla)

a: beams are being set into them
p: A building method of the time: courses of wood laid between courses of stone, as in Solomon's courtyard.
b: Cyrus's memorandum gives the same pattern: three courses of large stones and one of timber (6:4). Solomon built his inner courtyard "with three layers of cut stone and a layer of cedar beams" (1 Kings 6:36). Timber courses in stone walls are known from buildings across the ancient Near East, from Ugarit to Anatolia. They tied the stones together and may have helped walls survive earthquakes. "Great blocks of stone" translates "stones of rolling," either stones too big to carry that were moved on rollers, or, from an Akkadian word, dressed stone; the Greek of Ezra has "choice stones" (Rahlfs, checked).

a: We are servants of the God of the heavens and the earth.
p: Not as a people or a party, but as servants of the God of heaven and earth, rebuilding an ancient house.
b: The elders answer an official's question with a short history lesson (5:11–16). They name their God in terms a Persian could accept, the God of the heavens and the earth (compare Jonah 1:9; Genesis 24:3). They claim an old right, not a new one: "a king of Israel, a great one," Solomon, built this house long ago (1 Kings 6:1). They confess that the exile was their ancestors' fault (5:12). And they rest their case on Cyrus's decree (5:13–15). Commentators admire the answer's mix of faith and diplomacy. It never mentions Zerubbabel, perhaps to avoid drawing attention to a descendant of David.

a: because our ancestors angered the God of the heavens
p: The elders tell a Persian official what the prophets taught: Judah fell because of its own sin.
b: This is the Bible's standard explanation of the exile, told in Kings and Chronicles: "They, though, made fun of God's messengers. They looked down on his words and jeered at his prophets, till the LORD's fury came up against his people, till there was no cure" (2 Chronicles 36:16). Nebuchadnezzar is only God's instrument. The same confession returns in Ezra's prayer (9:7) and in Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9. "The Chaldean" names Nebuchadnezzar's people, the ruling group of southern Babylonia.

a: Cyrus king of Babylon
p: Cyrus took the old title of Babylon's kings. Babylonian contracts of his reign date by 'Cyrus, king of Babylon.'
b: After taking Babylon in 539 BC, Cyrus presented himself as the legitimate heir of its kings. The Cyrus Cylinder calls him "king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad," and business tablets of his reign are dated by "Cyrus, king of Babylon, king of the lands." So the elders' phrase is exactly right for the time. His "first year" as king of Babylon began in the spring of 538 BC.

a: He laid the foundations of God's house in Jerusalem
p: Here Sheshbazzar lays the foundation. In 3:8–10 it is Zerubbabel and Jeshua. Readers have explained this in several ways.
b: One man: some traditional readers take Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel as the same person, the official Babylonian name and the family name. Two men, two roles: Sheshbazzar, the official governor appointed by Cyrus, is credited by the elders because he held the royal commission, while Zerubbabel did the work (3:8), as many commentators say. Two foundings: Sheshbazzar began under Cyrus, the work stopped, and Zerubbabel founded it again in 520 (Haggai 2:18). Many critical scholars add that the elders' claim of continuous building "from then until now" is diplomatic, since 4:24 says the work stopped. The elders needed Cyrus's man, not David's heir, to make their legal case. See 1:8 and the topic on Sheshbazzar.

a: the king's treasure house there in Babylon
p: Persian records were kept in treasuries. Thousands of tablets from Persepolis show how thorough the record-keeping was.
b: The Aramaic is "the house of the treasures of the king." Persian treasuries stored precious goods along with documents. At Persepolis, Darius's capital in Persia, archaeologists found thousands of clay tablets in the Fortification and Treasury buildings, recording payments and rations in Elamite and Aramaic. Tattenai suggests a search in Babylon, where Cyrus had issued his decree; the document turns up in Ecbatana instead (6:2). The request treats the Jews' claim fairly: if Cyrus said so, Darius should honor it.

a: In Ecbatana, the fortress in the province of Media
p: Cyrus spent summers in Ecbatana, so a memo from his first year being filed there makes sense.
b: Ecbatana, modern Hamadan in Iran, was the old capital of the Medes. Greek writers say Cyrus and later kings spent the summer there and the winter in Babylon (Xenophon, Cyropaedia 8.6.22), and Herodotus describes its fortress with seven rings of walls (Herodotus 1.98). If Cyrus issued his order in the summer of 538 BC, a record could well have been filed there rather than in Babylon. Many historians count this unexpected detail as an argument for the document's authenticity: a forger in Jerusalem would more likely have said Babylon. The Greek of Ezra did not keep the name, writing "in a city, in the fortress of the city of the Medes" (Rahlfs, checked). The Aramaic name is Achmetha (Old Persian Hagmatana); Ecbatana is its Greek form.

a: For the record:
p: The heading of an archive note. A similar memorandum allowed the Jews of Elephantine to rebuild their temple.
b: Dikhronah, "memorandum" or "record," is the heading of an official note, not a letter: it has no address or greeting. A striking parallel comes from Elephantine in Egypt. After their temple there was destroyed in 410 BC, the Jewish garrison petitioned the Persian governor of Judah, Bagohi (Bagavahya). The reply survives as a "memorandum" of what Bagavahya and Delaiah, the son of Sanballat of Samaria, said: the "altar house" of the God of heaven could be rebuilt "on its site, as it was before," and offerings brought there. Its form and wording are close to 6:3–5.

a: It is to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide
p: Sixty by sixty cubits would be three times as wide as Solomon's Temple. The length is missing.
b: A cubit was about 18 inches, so sixty cubits is about 90 feet. Solomon's house "measured sixty cubits in length, twenty in width and thirty cubits in height" (1 Kings 6:2). The memo gives height and width but no length, and both figures are odd. Many scholars think the text has been damaged and that it originally gave the length, perhaps as sixty, and a smaller width. Others think the figures were limits on what the king would pay for, not a plan. Haggai's words about the new house looking "like nothing" (Haggai 2:3) suggest it was not built larger than the first. 1 Esdras 6:24 has the same two numbers, and no ancient witness gives a length.

a: The cost is to be given out of the king's house.
p: Persian kings did pay to restore shrines in conquered lands. Darius did so in Egypt as well.
b: The memorandum promises that the royal treasury will pay, and Darius orders the payments made from the taxes of Beyond the River (6:8). The Egyptian official Udjahorresnet, on his statue now in the Vatican, says Darius sent him to restore the "House of Life," the temple school, at Sais, and Cyrus claimed on his Cylinder to have restored the shrines of Babylonia. Funding local temples was a way to win loyalty and to have local gods' priests pray for the king (6:10). Some historians doubt that the empire really paid for the whole building, since Haggai describes the people working with their own resources (Haggai 1:8).

a: keep away from there
p: 'Be far from there' is the formula of Aramaic legal documents for giving up a claim or not interfering.
b: The Aramaic rachiqin havo min-tammah is literally "be far from there." In property deeds from Elephantine, a seller declares "I have withdrawn from you" (literally "I am far from you") to give up any claim. So Darius's words are more than a warning to step back. They are an official order not to interfere with the project. The decree changes Tattenai's role from inspector to paymaster (6:8).

a: The Jews' governor
p: The governor is not named. Zerubbabel drops out of the record about this time, and no one knows why.
b: Haggai calls Zerubbabel "governor of Judah" (Haggai 1:1), so he is probably the unnamed governor here, but Ezra 5–6 never names him after 5:2, and Ezra does not name him at the dedication (6:16–18). Haggai had said God would make him "like a seal ring, for I have chosen you" (Haggai 2:23), and Zechariah spoke of "a man whose name is Branch... he will build the LORD's temple" (Zechariah 6:12, translated fresh). Some historians have guessed that hopes for a new Davidic king alarmed the Persians, who removed him. Others say there is no evidence of that: he may simply have died or finished his term. Later Jewish tradition identified him with Nehemiah (Bavli Sanhedrin 38a). See the topic on Zerubbabel.

a: with care
p: The word means 'exactly, diligently.' The Plain English Translation gives it the same English each time it appears in chapters 5–6.
b: Asparna is a Persian loanword meaning "exactly, diligently, in full." Tattenai uses it of the elders' building (5:8), Darius uses it here and at the end of his decree (6:12), and the officials then act on it (6:13). It returns in Artaxerxes' letter to Ezra (7:17, 7:21, 7:26). The Plain English Translation renders it "with care" each time in chapters 5–6, so the reader can see that the officials are to pay as carefully as the elders build. The next phrase, "so that they are not held up," is literally "that there be no stopping."

a: sacrifices of soothing smell
p: The Aramaic uses the Torah's word for sacrifices that please God, 'soothing' ones.
b: The Aramaic nichochin is the same word as the Hebrew re'ach nichoach, "soothing smell," the phrase the law uses for offerings that God accepts with pleasure. It first appears after the flood: "The LORD smelled the soothing smell" (Genesis 8:21). A Persian king using it suggests that a Jewish adviser helped draft the decree, as with Artaxerxes in 7:12–26. Daniel 2:46 uses the same word of offerings to Daniel.

a: pray for the life of the king and of his sons
p: Persian kings wanted local priests to pray for them. Jeremiah had told the exiles to pray for their city.
b: The Cyrus Cylinder ends by asking that the gods Cyrus had returned to their shrines should daily ask Bel and Nabu for long life for him and his son. Darius wants the same from the God of the heavens. The Jews of Elephantine promised Bagohi that if he helped them, they would offer sacrifices and pray for him. Jeremiah had already told the exiles: "Seek the peace of the city I sent you to as exiles, and pray for it to the LORD" (Jeremiah 29:7, translated fresh). The Mishnah says, "Pray for the welfare of the government" (Mishnah Avot 3:2), and Paul urged prayer "for kings and for all who hold high office" (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Synagogues and churches still pray for their governments.

a: he is to be lifted up and impaled on it
p: The KJV says 'hanged.' The punishment meant is impaling on a sharpened beam, a Persian practice.
b: The Aramaic yitmeche means "be struck" or "fixed" on the beam. The KJV's "let him be hanged thereon" can suggest a noose. Persian kings impaled rebels: Darius says at Behistun that he impaled the rebel leaders, and Herodotus reports that he impaled three thousand Babylonians (Herodotus 3.159). The same punishment is probably meant in Esther, where Haman builds a "tree" fifty cubits high (Esther 5:14; Esther 7:9–10). Turning the guilty man's house into a dunghill is another curse of the time, found also in Daniel 2:5 and 3:29.

a: May the God who has made his name live there
t: The place where God's name lives
p: A Persian decree speaks in the language of Deuteronomy about the place God chose.
b: Deuteronomy promises that "the LORD your God will choose a place to make his name live there" (Deuteronomy 12:11; compare Deuteronomy 16:2). Kings and Chronicles identify the place as Jerusalem's Temple (1 Kings 8:29; 2 Chronicles 6:20). Darius's decree uses the same phrase, probably because Jewish scribes helped write it. The curse at the end of a decree, calling on a god to punish any who change it, is common in royal inscriptions, including Darius's own at Behistun. See the topic on the place the LORD will choose.
r: Deuteronomy 12:5; Deuteronomy 12:11; Deuteronomy 16:2; 1 Kings 8:29; 1 Kings 9:3; 2 Chronicles 6:20; Nehemiah 1:9

a: and Artaxerxes king of Persia
p: Artaxerxes reigned decades after the Temple was finished. The writer looks ahead to his gifts in chapter 7.
b: The Temple was finished under Darius (6:15). Artaxerxes I came to the throne in 465 BC, fifty years later. Most readers think the writer here sums up the whole Persian support for the house, including Artaxerxes' later gifts and his decree for Ezra (7:15–24; 7:27). Three kings, Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes, stand behind it, as "the God of Israel" stands above them all; the verse's double "by the order of" puts God's order first. Some think a later editor added the name. The Greek of Ezra keeps it. On 4:6–23 the same king is the one who stopped the walls, so the book shows him first as opponent and then as patron.

a: in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius
p: Darius's sixth year ran from 516 to 515 BC. The Temple stood about seventy years after it was burned.
b: The third of Adar, the twelfth month, in Darius's sixth year was about March 12, 515 BC. The first Temple had burned in 586 BC, so the new one was finished about seventy years later. Zechariah had asked how long God would be angry with Jerusalem "these seventy years" (Zechariah 1:12, translated fresh), and many readers see here one way of counting Jeremiah's seventy years. The second Temple stood until the Romans destroyed it in AD 70, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod from about 20 BC (John 2:20). In Jewish history the whole period is named "the Second Temple period."

a: joyfully held the dedication of this house of God
p: The Aramaic word is the one behind the later feast of Hanukkah, which rededicated this same Temple in 164 BC.
b: Chanukkah means dedication, used of the altar in the wilderness (Numbers 7:84) and of Solomon's Temple (2 Chronicles 7:9). When Judas Maccabeus cleansed this second Temple after its defilement by Antiochus IV, Jews kept eight days of dedication, the feast still kept as Hanukkah (1 Maccabees 4:52–59). John 10:22 mentions Jesus in the Temple at "the feast of dedication." Compared with Solomon's dedication, when "Solomon gave twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep" (1 Kings 8:63), this one is small, but it is kept with the same joy.
r: Numbers 7:84; 1 Kings 8:63; 2 Chronicles 7:5–9; Nehemiah 12:27; 1 Maccabees 4:52–59; John 10:22

a: 12 male goats as a sin offering for all Israel
p: Only a few tribes came back, but the offering is made for all twelve. The returnees stand for all Israel.
b: A sin offering (chatta'ah, which some scholars call a "purification offering") cleansed the people and the sanctuary. Twelve goats, one for each tribe, recall the twelve leaders' offerings at the first altar's dedication (Numbers 7:87) and anticipate Ezra's own twelve bulls and twelve goats "for all Israel" (8:35). The community is small and mostly from Judah, Benjamin and Levi (1:5), yet it acts for the whole people. Jewish and Christian readers alike have seen in this a hope that the scattered tribes would be gathered again (Ezekiel 37:15–22; Matthew 19:28).

a: according to what is written in the book of Moses
t: What the book of Moses says
p: The law sets the priests' and Levites' duties, though the twenty-four divisions come from David's time.
b: The Torah gives the duties of priests and Levites (Numbers 3–4; Numbers 8; Numbers 18), but not the divisions; Chronicles credits those to David (1 Chronicles 23–24). Ezra's phrase probably means that the duties followed Moses while the arrangement followed custom. 6:18 is the last verse of the Aramaic section; the story returns to Hebrew in 6:19. Some think the writer switched back to Hebrew to tell the Passover in the language of the law.
r: Numbers 3:5–10; Numbers 8:5–26; Numbers 18:1–7; 1 Chronicles 23:6; 1 Chronicles 24:1–19; 2 Chronicles 35:4–5

a: The people of the exile kept the Passover
p: The first feast in the finished house is Passover, the feast of the first exodus, as after Hezekiah's and Josiah's reforms.
b: The fourteenth of the first month (Nisan) came about six weeks after the dedication. Passover marks new beginnings in Israel's story: the exodus (Exodus 12), the entry into the land (Joshua 5:10), and the reforms of Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 30) and Josiah (2 Kings 23:21–23; 2 Chronicles 35). Here it seals the return from Babylon as a second exodus (see 1:6). An Aramaic papyrus from Elephantine dated 419 BC, often called the Passover Papyrus, passes on instructions for keeping the Feast of Unleavened Bread in Nisan to the Jewish garrison there.
r: Exodus 12:1–20; Joshua 5:10; 2 Chronicles 30:1–27; 2 Chronicles 35:1–19; 2 Kings 23:21–23; Leviticus 23:5–8

a: They slaughtered the Passover
p: In Exodus each household slaughtered its own lamb. In the Temple period the Levites did it for the people.
b: Exodus says "the whole assembled community of Israel will slaughter it" (Exodus 12:6), each family with its own lamb. At Hezekiah's Passover the Levites took over for those who were unclean (2 Chronicles 30:17), and Josiah gave the job to the Levites (2 Chronicles 35:6). The Hebrew here only says "they," following "the priests and the Levites"; many translations specify the Levites. The care for purity (6:20) and the joining of outsiders (6:21) both echo Hezekiah's Passover.

a: everyone who had separated himself to them from the uncleanness of the nations of the land
p: The community that turned away outsiders (4:3) welcomes anyone who separates himself to seek the LORD.
b: The verse names two groups: the returned exiles and "everyone who had separated himself to them." Many scholars think the second group means people of the land, Judeans or northern Israelites who had never been deported, who now committed themselves to the community's way of life. Others think it means converts from other peoples, like the foreigner of Exodus 12:48 who may keep the Passover once circumcised. Either way the door is open to those who separate from "the uncleanness of the nations." The same verb, "separate," returns sharply in chapters 9–10, where the issue is marriage (9:1; 10:11). The balance between welcome and separation runs through the whole book.

a: the Assyrian king's heart
p: Darius is called 'the king of Assyria.' This is not a mistake but a way of naming the empire that ruled the old Assyrian lands.
b: Persia's empire included the old heartland of Assyria, and writers of the period sometimes used the old name for the whole region (Herodotus calls Babylon a city of "Assyria," 1.178). The title also carries a message. Assyria was the empire that first scattered Israel (2 Kings 17:6); now "the king of Assyria" helps them rebuild. Nehemiah's prayer speaks of hardship "since the days of the kings of Assyria until this day" (Nehemiah 9:32). And it is the LORD who turned the king's heart: "Like water in irrigation ditches, the king's heart lies in the LORD's hand; / he steers it wherever he likes" (Proverbs 21:1). "To give their hands strength" is the opposite of 4:4.
